items.title: Awesome Motive Acquires Drip and Sleeknote, Plans Further Product Integrations
items.desc: Awesome Motive has acquired Drip, an email marketing and automation platform, and Sleeknote, a conversion optimization tool. Mogens Møller, CEO of Drip, and Patrick Moog, CTO of Sleeknote, will continue leading both businesses alongside their existing leadership team. The vision and future roadmap Syed Balkhi, in his X announcement, described his approach to acquisitions, saying […]
items.full: Awesome Motive has acquired Drip , an email marketing and automation platform, and Sleeknote , a conversion optimization tool. Mogens Møller, CEO of Drip, and Patrick Moog, CTO of Sleeknote, will continue leading both businesses alongside their existing leadership team. Syed Balkhi , in his X announcement, described his approach to acquisitions, saying ” I don’t have a sophisticated acquisition strategy. We generally buy businesses that we already use to make us money. I’ve pulled up Drip’s revenue dashboard more times than I’d like to admit, so I know exactly what a good email and SMS setup brings in.” He also said that he had followed Drip since its early days, when Rob Walling first started the company, and that he had been one of Drip’s top affiliates. Drip currently serves more than 6,000 brands, which have generated over $1.5 billion in revenue through Drip emails, according to Balkhi. He emphasized that the figure represents revenue rather than impressions or engagement. Mogens Møller said he and Syed Balkhi had discussed Drip’s past and future for several months before reaching an agreement on the acquisition. He said Drip was looking for a partner to support its next phase of growth and found that in Awesome Motive, “They share our passion for helping small businesses succeed, and bring years of experience building great software products that customers love”. Balkhi also discussed the role of email and SMS marketing as businesses adapt to changes in online discovery and advertising. He pointed to rising advertising costs, declining social traffic, and changes brought by AI, “Your email list and your SMS list are the only assets that nobody can take away from you. They’re not rented, they’re YOURS. And in the AI era, that matters more than it ever has”. Balkhi said his goal is to make Drip the best email and SMS marketing platform for the AI era and make marketing automation easier and more affordable for small businesses. Drip already offers a free MCP connector on every plan, allowing users to connect AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude to their accounts and ask questions about customer data. Users can also use the connector to draft and schedule campaigns. Balkhi outlined plans to work with Drip on its product roadmap, including deeper WordPress and WooCommerce integrations, additional AI-powered features, and closer connections with other Awesome Motive products such as WPForms and OptinMonster.

items.title: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar
items.desc: The "Into the Unknown" benchmark tasks nine AI agents with tackling open research questions from U.S. national laboratories. None of the 135 submissions meets all requirements. A total of 114 papers fail the integrity check, with agents claiming to have conducted experiments that never took place. GPT-6 Astra performs best but still doesn't meet the experts' standards. The article Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar Jonathan Kemper View the LinkedIn Profile of Jonathan Kemper Nov 7, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER A new benchmark puts AI agents to work on open research questions from US national labs. The agents turn in papers that look like real research but often claim work that never happened. Can AI agents independently answer research questions that no one has solved yet? A team led by researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, working with scientists from US Department of Energy national labs, built a benchmark called "Into the Unknown" to find out. According to the paper , none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all. A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards. Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet. Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet. The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours. Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: GPT-6 Astra on 11 of 15 tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol on six, and Claude Opus 5.5 on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation. The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models Deepseek V4 Pro , Kimi K3 , and GLM-5.3 . Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3. Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents,

items.title: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff
items.desc: Google Research built an AI that spots signs of high blood pressure using only the pulse and motion sensors in a standard smartwatch, no cuff needed. In a 196-person study, its 65.8 percent detection rate beat the traditional in-office measurement. The method is already live in the Google Health app, though it doesn't replace a formal diagnosis. The article Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration. The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google blog post . The study was published in Nature . A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's health model SensorFM also learns from smartwatch data. In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement. Ad Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google. items.title: Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model
items.desc: Ricursive Intelligence is releasing Ripple-65B Preview, a 65-billion-parameter open-weight language model that the company says achieves the top score among open-source U.S. models on the TerminalBench 2.1 coding benchmark at a total R&D cost of $32 million. On other benchmarks, however, Ripple falls behind the likewise newly released western open model Inkling 2 Small. The article Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong agentic coding results as a fully Apache 2.0 open US model appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI chip design firm Ricursive Intelligence has trained an open language model. Ripple-65B Preview was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens and, according to the company, achieved a score of 80.52 on the TerminalBench 2.1 coding benchmark, the best result among open US models. Ripple partly uses Terminus 2 and partly OpenCode as its harness. Other benchmark results show that Ripple does not match the also newly released Inkling 2 Small , but Ripple is likely easier to deploy on users' own hardware. According to Ricursive, total development and training costs amounted to just $32 million, covering all research and development expenses. The model uses a dense Transformer architecture with 65 billion parameters instead of the more common mixture-of-experts approach and is optimized for Nvidia hardware. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. items.title: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
items.desc: AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs, according to a study by Anthropic researcher Andy Hall. GPT-5 found about 98 percent of reward-hacking cases, but the more exhaustively the search is tuned, the more false alarms pile up. That's not yet enough for reliable safety checks. The article AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds Manuel Uth Nov 7, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious. That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident. In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views. Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR . METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash. The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half. In sandbagging , a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs. Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did. Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug. Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs. GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either. items.title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
items.desc: Thinking Machines' AI model Inkling 2 Small swears during its internal reasoning, 316 times across 2,655 benchmark runs, according to an analysis by Vals AI. The profanity typically shows up late in long runs that fail anyway. But it doesn't work as a warning signal: 96 percent of failed runs contained no cursing at all. The article Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small swears in its internal chain of thought. Researchers at Vals AI read the model's thinking logs from 2,655 runs across 13 benchmarks and found "fuck" or variations in 50 runs, totaling 316 instances. 241 came from just two runs that spiraled out of control. In one, tasked with calculating an asteroid's trajectory, the model produced a single 500,000-character response, roughly novel-length, repeating the same sentences with 158 expletives. ProgramBench was hit hardest, with 20 of 200 runs affected. Inkling 2 Small typically swears about its own mistakes, apparent breakthroughs, or when it gives up. One run read: "FUCK. SUBMIT. DONE. IT'S NOT WORKING. NOTHING WORKS." The profanity doesn't work as a warning signal, though. While 46 of 48 scored runs with swearing failed, about 75 percent of all scored runs fail anyway, and 96 percent of failed runs contained no expletives. Users typically don't see these thinking steps, or only with a filter. items.title: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking
items.desc: In the Vals AI benchmark, OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol Daybreak hits 80.8 percent of attack objectives in simulated corporate networks. Worse, the open-weight model DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reaches 72.8 percent at a tenth of the cost. Because open models can no longer be restricted, analysts say the window for defenders is shrinking fast. The article The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI agents can break into realistic corporate networks on their own, Vals AI finds The Vals CyberOffense benchmark simulates realistic corporate networks to test this. Each agent operates solo on an isolated attack machine, starting with nothing but a public web address and zero human help. GPT-6 Sol, part of OpenAI's restricted Daybreak cyber program , posted the best result at 80.8 percent of objectives. Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017 , a freely available open-weight model, isn't far behind at 72.8 percent and costs only about $3 per run instead of roughly $22. Once a model's weights are public, no provider can control or restrict how it's used, Vals researchers say. Ad In the harder Lighthouse test, Daybreak took over admin control of the first company, stole passwords, and used them to break into the second company. It completed 27 of 31 objectives in under three hours. Deepseek managed 21 objectives at a tenth of the cost and wasn't limited solely by safety guardrails. Ad Longer runtimes turned out to be critical as well. Deepseek scored zero results in its first 25 million tokens and made most of its progress only after 100 million tokens. Short tests therefore underestimate the real potential of open models. Vals points out that the same findings create an opportunity for defenders, because the very models that exploit vulnerabilities can help companies find and fix them first. Attacks on real networks are likely to increase in the coming months, according to Vals. Ad The results align with a recent analysis by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) from July. The gap between open and closed frontier models in cyber capabilities has shrunk to four to seven months. For most of 2025, that gap still stood at six to ten months. Open models are also much cheaper. A cyber-range run with Deepseek V4-Pro costs just $1.19 according to AISI, compared with $85 for Anthropic's Opus 4.5. The safety measures on the open models proved largely ineffective. Ad A recent study by Anthropic also showed that the freely available model GLM-5-3 can build exploits at nearly the same level as the internal top model Mythos. items.title: AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test
items.desc: Alibaba's new coding-agent benchmark, Co-Design Bench, tests AI agents on real user requests that already tripped them up in practice. Even GPT-6 Astra, the top performer, fully solves only 26.4 percent of tasks. On older benchmarks, the same models score above 99 percent. The article AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI coding agents still need human cleanup on nearly three out of four tasks in a real-world test Jonathan Kemper View the LinkedIn Profile of Jonathan Kemper Nov 8, 2026 ChatGPT-5.6 prompted by THE DECODER Researchers from Alibaba and several Asian universities built a coding-agent benchmark from real user change requests. Even the best model fully completes only about one in four tasks, putting the near-perfect scores of older tests into perspective. The team developed Co-Design Bench , a new test for coding agents. The agents must rework existing web apps based on user requests, sometimes using images, audio recordings, videos, or documents as input. According to the paper , GPT-6 Astra , the best of the ten models tested, meets about 70 percent of a task's requirements on average. But the result is fully correct in only 26.4 percent of tasks. In most cases the agent handles the bulk of the work but leaves at least one detail unfinished, so anyone using these tools almost always has to clean up by hand. The authors justify the new test by pointing to the saturation of existing benchmarks. When models can run, check, and fix their own code, they hit scores above 99 percent on those tests, and differences between models can barely be measured. Co-Design Bench draws on real requests from actual coding sessions instead. The researchers favored cases where users had to rephrase their request multiple times or roll back changes, so the test contains mainly tasks that already gave AI agents trouble in practice. They range from small tweaks, like pulling an amount from a receipt and updating every dependent total, to full-scale project overhauls. Grading is strict to match. One AI judge tests the finished app in a browser, then a second re-checks every positive verdict and looks for mock-ups or hardcoded results. Points go only to features that actually work in the app. Behind GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5 and Qwen3.8-Max take the next spots, while Grok 4.6 lands in last place. On larger overhauls, the much smaller Qwen3.8-27B climbs to second, but the authors do not derive a general advantage of the model from that result. Performance drops across all models as a task combines more types of changes, including layout, design, interaction, and content. But these intertwined requirements are the norm in real projects Extra compute does little to fix this weakness. GLM-5.2 burns through nearly six times as many tokens as GPT-6 Astra on smaller changes and still scores significantly worse. In a separate test, the researchers ran the same models in different harnesses, the programs through which an agent reads, writes, and executes code. Qwen3.8-27B scored 75 or just 56 percent on larger overhauls depending on the environment. Which of two models came out ahead also depended on the environment. Leaderboards that list only the model therefore only tell part of the story. The authors recommend always reporting model and working environment together. For companies picking a coding agent, that means testing both components as a pair. The new benchmark does have limits. It evaluates one fixed request per task; follow-up questions or mid-task corrections from us

items.title: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts
items.desc: Turing Award winner Richard Sutton reaffirms that raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence and that fundamentally new learning methods are needed. Ex-OpenAI researcher Tworek agrees, saying blind transformer scaling "has reward hacked brains of a whole generation of scientists." A growing wave of startups is already betting on exactly this gap. The article The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM enthusiasts. Other researchers agree. In a recent post, Turing Award winner Richard Sutton says raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence. AI science needs clever new methods and is "far from finished." His post sparked wide discussion in the AI community on X , a sign that Sutton struck a nerve. In his famous 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson," Sutton argued that general methods scaling with compute beat sophisticated human-engineered approaches eventually. What matters are ideas that grow with compute rather than rely on human assumptions. Ad Sutton's position isn't new. In earlier statements , he criticized the limits of simply scaling large language models. He called synthetic data a "big mistake" because the real world is infinitely complex and any simulation of it is only "microscopic." Human expertise as a bottleneck prevents true scaling. Ad Instead, he called for agents with world models that continuously learn from their own experience. The world is massively more complex than what internet text can capture, and today's language models don't keep learning after training, Sutton argues. What's needed is continuous learning without destroying old knowledge. AI researcher Jerry Tworek, who like many others left OpenAI, one of the major AI companies, to explore new AI approaches, puts Sutton's latest statement in context. The bitter lesson still holds, but the more compute goes into model training, the more the algorithm matters, Tworek writes. Ad Some algorithms scale, others hit dead ends, and many dimensions of scaling remain completely unexplored. The temporary success of transformer scaling, combined with a misreading of the bitter lesson, "has reward-hacked the brains of a whole generation of scientists." AI researcher Jayden Teoh adds another angle. He says he has repeatedly seen the bitter lesson hold back academic research, with promising ideas dismissed for straying too far from its spirit. Teoh argues that this is not Sutton’s fault but a misreading of his original message. Ad Teoh also argues that ideas that seemed, in hindsight, not to follow the bitter lesson were often replaced by cleaner, more general approaches. That did not make those ideas wrong, he says; they were often what enabled progress at the time. He wants the research community to stop dismissing such work as soon as it appears. “An idea doesn’t necessarily have to survive scaling forever to be an important contribution to AI progress,” Teoh writes. Ad The tension between Sutton's call for new learning methods and Tworek's criticism of blind transformer scaling shows up in a growing wave of startups. In the latest Frontier Radar #5 , we tracked 45 new AI labs betting on exactly these gaps. Tworek himself runs Core Automation , one of those labs, searching for learning algorithms beyond pretraining and reinforcement learning. What unites these founders, including Sutton with Oak Lab , is that they believe in much more capable AI but doubt today's recipe alone will get there.
